findings.title: Periodic DNS queries: 10.0.19.14 → wpad.burnincandle.com every ~545s
findings.description: 10.0.19.14 queried wpad.burnincandle.com 41 times at a mean interval of 544.7s (CV=0.30).
findings.explanation: Regular DNS lookups of the same name can be DNS-based C2 (queries carry no data here, but the schedule does) or plain background software behavior. Judge together with the resolved addresses and any tunneling indicators.

findings.title: Possible covert-channel candidate: http request header count of 10.0.19.14
findings.description: The request header count field across 18 HTTP messages from 10.0.19.14 varies over a small alphabet (6, 7, 3, 4) in a low-cardinality (4-state) repeated sequence. Mapping the values to bits and grouping 8 per byte yields 4 bytes that decode to printable-looking output (100%).
findings.explanation: Protocol metadata fields that the sender can freely choose (HTTP version, query type, TTL, port…) can carry hidden information by *value selection*: every packet is legal on its own, and only the sequence encodes data. This is an indicator, not proof — the same variation can occur naturally (client pools, load balancers). Judge by whether the decoded output is meaningful and whether the pattern persists. Full derivation: `netsleuth covert <pcap>`.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: http.request && ip.src == 10.0.19.14 — read the field of each packet in order, note the values (the engine observed: 3×1, 6×12, 4×1, 7×4), assign bits per the mapping and decode 8 bits per byte.

mitre.name: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
mitre.why: information encoded into protocol field choices rather than payload

mitre.why: application/protocol metadata used as a covert data channel

findings.title: Host sweep: 10.0.19.14 contacted 41 hosts on port 443
findings.description: 10.0.19.14 attempted connections to 41 distinct destination hosts, all on port 443 (https).
findings.explanation: Contacting many hosts on a single port is the signature of a host sweep looking for one vulnerable service (or of network discovery tooling). Compare with the port-scan finding: a port scan hits many ports on one host, a sweep hits one port on many hosts.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: ip.src == 10.0.19.14 && tcp.dstport == 443 — count the distinct ip.dst values.

mitre.name: Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks
mitre.why: scanning many IP addresses on one service port

findings.title: ICMP echo requests carrying 32 bytes of data payload
findings.description: 1 echo request(s) carry payloads of 32+ bytes (normal ping payloads are usually small and uniform).
findings.explanation: The ping protocol has no business carrying rich text/binary data. Large or varied payloads inside ICMP echo are how simple backdoors exfiltrate or beacon while slipping past port-based rules. Some monitoring tools do embed data, so read the payload before judging.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: icmp && data.len >= 16, then inspect the echo data field.

mitre.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
mitre.why: ICMP echo used as a data channel

mitre.why: data moved over an unencrypted non-application protocol
